title: Auditors and super funds put on notice
full_text:
The corporate regulator has put super funds and auditors on notice over shabby valuation practices for unlisted assets.
The Australian Securities & Investments Commission on Wednesday released its second report card on the super industry’s financial reports and audits, finding once again there was not enough scrutiny of asset valuations, with too much reliance on external managers’ valuations.
ASIC commissioner Kate O’Rourke said there had been improvements in some areas on a year ago, but not enough.
“Millions of Australians entrust superannuation trustees with their retirement savings. It’s imperative those investments are valued accurately, and auditors provide effective scrutiny to detect any unreliable investment valuations,” she said.
“Getting valuations right matters. Accurate investment valuations are particularly important as they directly affect members’ account balances, reported investment returns, fees charged and therefore retirement outcomes.
“Trustees cannot outsource responsibility for ensuring investment valuations are accurate and reliable, even where external fund managers are involved.” Last year, ASIC similarly found inconsistent fund disclosures as well as unreliable valuations, with auditors simply accepting the valuations handed over by external fund managers.
Of 33 investments ASIC sought information on this year, funds were able to provide a valuation model or an independent valuation report on just seven.
“Our finding was that for two audit surveillances, the auditor didn’t have sufficient audit evidence for some of those internally managed investments,” Ms O’Rourke said.
The regulator has since issued notices to four auditors from three of the audit firms included in its surveillance, setting out its findings and concerns. All auditors have proposed remedial measures.
The audit firms surveilled were BDO, Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC. Worryingly, ASIC also found funds delayed reflecting significant asset writedowns on members’ account balances.
In some cases, members’ balances were not updated to reflect the writedowns until the following financial year, Ms O’Rourke said.
The regulator is now probing this line of inquiry further due to the prospect of members potentially paying too high fees in a given year.
“We saw there was a gap there in the accounting treatment, so that it was done in a different financial year, and that has fee consequences for the member,” Ms O’Rourke said. “That’s something we’re making further inquiries into.” The fresh review of funds’ practices around unlisted assets comes amid heightened scrutiny of the private credit sector from both investors and regulators.
Ms O’Rourke said ASIC now plans to review the financial reports of a further 20 super funds and 20 managed investment schemes.
Funds’ oversight of managed investment schemes has been in the spotlight for the past year as the Shield and First Guardian scandals exposed glaring gaps in monitoring everything from fund flows to underlying investments. More than 3000 managed investment schemes are on offer to investors in the market.
